3	import (
4		"context"
5		"encoding/json"
6	)
7	
8	// externalAgentsRejectionNotLocal and ...NotVerified explain why an
9	// external_agents grant was dropped. They mirror the OPF command's reasons
10	// because the hazard is the same one: a JSON settings diff that grants
11	// execution does not read as executable to a reviewer.
12	const (
13		externalAgentsRejectionNotLocal   = "it did not come from .entire/settings.local.json"
14		externalAgentsRejectionUnverified = "the local settings file could not be verified as untracked"
15	)
16	
17	// enforceExternalAgentsTrust drops external_agents unless it came from a local
18	// file positively verified as this developer's own.
19	//
20	// external_agents is not a preference. It turns on the $PATH scan that globs
21	// for entire-agent-* binaries and runs each one's "info" subcommand, and it
22	// keeps running them for every hook thereafter. Honoring it from the
23	// version-controlled .entire/settings.json would let an ordinary pull request
24	// pair `{"external_agents": true}` with a binary committed next to it (or
25	// merely present on a shared machine's $PATH) and get it executed on every
26	// developer who pulls. The reasoning in enforceOPFCommandTrust applies
27	// unchanged: one line of JSON is a poor place to hide an exec grant, and there
28	// is no prompt in front of this one at all.
29	//
30	// localData is the raw local-file bytes, nil when the file is absent or its
31	// layer was dropped as tracked. The deep (index AND HEAD) check is used and
32	// localOwn is required: like the OPF command and unlike the layer as a whole,
33	// an unverifiable repository fails CLOSED, because being wrong means running
34	// someone else's binary rather than losing a preference.
35	//
36	// Rejection is a downgrade, never an error. Discovery simply does not run, and
37	// the user's own agents are unaffected — the interactive setup flows call
38	// DiscoverAndRegisterAlways and reach external plugins regardless, so the
39	// remedy stays available from the command that needs it.
40	func enforceExternalAgentsTrust(ctx context.Context, s *EntireSettings, localSettingsPath string, localData []byte) {
41		// Only a true value grants anything, so only a true value is gated.
42		// Warning about a false one would be noise about a privilege nobody asked
43		// for.
44		if s == nil || !s.ExternalAgents {
45			return
46		}
47	
48		var reason string
49		switch {
50		case !localSetsExternalAgents(localData):
51			reason = externalAgentsRejectionNotLocal
52		case classifyLocalSettingsDeep(ctx, localSettingsPath) != localOwn:
53			reason = externalAgentsRejectionUnverified
54		default:
55			return
56		}
57	
58		// Recorded rather than logged, for the reasons in enforceOPFCommandTrust:
59		// the loader runs while the log level is still being resolved, and a line
60		// in .entire/logs is not a signal the user sees.
61		s.externalAgentsRejection = reason
62		s.ExternalAgents = false
63	}
64	
65	// localSetsExternalAgents reports whether the local override file explicitly
66	// sets external_agents.
67	//
68	// Presence of the key is what matters, not the merged value: both files may
69	// set true, and comparing effective values after the merge would credit the
70	// project layer for the local file's grant. A malformed local file yields
71	// false, the safe direction — the merge reports the parse error separately.
72	func localSetsExternalAgents(data []byte) bool {
73		var raw map[string]json.RawMessage
74		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &raw); err != nil {
75			return false
76		}
77		return rawHasKey(raw, "external_agents")
78	}

  The GitHub Copilot CLI provides granular control over tool, URL, and path permissions to ensure safe

  Tool Permissions:

  Tool availability is controlled via the --available-tools and --excluded-tools options. The --available-tools option
  disables all other tools; the --excluded-tools option disables only the specified tools. These filters decide which
  tools the model can see.

  Tool permissions are managed via --allow-tool, --deny-tool, and --allow-all-tools. Denial rules always take

  is optional and dependent on the kind. The following kinds are supported:

    shell(command:*?)
        Exactly matches a specific shell command to be run. If the command is omitted, all shell commands are allowed.
        In most cases, this will be an exact match against the command name. To match prefixes, use the :* suffix.

        basis, e.g. "git push" or "gh pr create". To match all git commands, use "shell(git:*)". Wildcard matching is
        performed on the stem of the command, so "shell(git:*)" will match "git push" but not "gitea".

    write(path?)
        Matches tools that create and modify files, except shell tool invocations. If the path is omitted, matches
        all such writes. A relative path matches by trailing path components, so "write(.env)" matches a file named

559:`external_agents` turns on the `$PATH` scan that looks for `entire-agent-*`

540	- **JSONL skip rules.** Entire skips scanning fields whose name *ends in* `signature` (so `thinkingSignature` too), fields ending in `id`/`ids`, and structural-path fields (`filepath`, `file_path`, `cwd`, `root`, `directory`, `dir`, `path`) to avoid false positives. Objects whose `type` starts with `image` or equals `base64` are also skipped — and that skip is what leaves a pasted image unredacted rather than merely unflagged. It matches some agents' image shapes and not others, which is why the outcome differs per agent: see [What Entire does NOT understand: pasted images and screenshots](#what-entire-does-not-understand-pasted-images-and-screenshots) above.
541	- **Built-in PII patterns are US-centric.** `phone` matches North American (NANP) formats only — international formats, including E.164 numbers outside `+1`, are not detected. `address` matches the street line only; city, state, and ZIP/postcode are preserved. If you handle personal data from other regions, add `custom_patterns` for your locale rather than relying on the built-in categories alone.
542	- **Custom PII patterns are user-authored.** Teams own the correctness of their `custom_patterns`. An invalid regex is logged and skipped, not enforced.
543	- **Users are ultimately responsible** for reviewing what they commit and push. Redaction is a safety net, not a guarantee.
544	
545	## Telemetry
546	
547	The CLI captures anonymous usage analytics by default. Sent to PostHog with `DisableGeoIP` enabled. Captured per command: command name, selected agent, whether Entire is enabled in the repo, CLI version, OS/arch, installed git version (best-effort; omitted if git is absent or unparseable), and **names** of flags passed (never their values). The distinct ID is a hashed machine identifier (`machineid.ProtectedID`), not a user identity.
548	
549	Not captured: flag values, prompt text, transcripts, file paths, repository identifiers, GitHub usernames, source code.
550	
551	Opt out via any one of:
552	
553	- `--telemetry=false` on a command that accepts it.
554	- `"telemetry": false` in `.entire/settings.json` or `.entire/settings.local.json`.
555	- `ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1` in the environment.
556	
557	## Why `external_agents` is local-only
558	
559	`external_agents` turns on the `$PATH` scan that looks for `entire-agent-*`
560	binaries and runs each one's `info` subcommand, then keeps running the ones it
561	registered for every hook thereafter. It is an execution grant, not a
562	preference, so it is honored under exactly the same rule as the OPF
563	[`command`](#why-command-is-local-only): only from `.entire/settings.local.json`,
564	and only when that file is untracked in both the index and `HEAD`. Reading it
565	from the committed `.entire/settings.json` would let an ordinary pull request
566	turn on execution of whatever `entire-agent-*` binary it could get onto a
567	developer's `$PATH`, and — as with `command` — one line of JSON does not read as
568	executable to a reviewer. There is no prompt in front of this one at all.
569	
570	Rejection is a downgrade, never an error: discovery simply does not run.
571	`entire status` names the setting and where it has to move, and the same reason
572	is logged. The interactive setup flows (`entire enable`, `entire configure`,
573	`entire agent add`, `entire plugin uninstall`) reach external agents regardless
574	of the setting, so the remedy stays available from the commands that need it —
575	and when one of them enables an external agent for you, it writes the setting to
576	`.entire/settings.local.json`, which is where it takes effect.
577	
578	Every `$PATH` scanner in the CLI also drops non-absolute entries. A relative
579	entry resolves against the process's working directory, which for a git hook is
580	whatever repository the caller was standing in, so a file committed to that
581	repository would otherwise be a binary Entire executes.

input.new_string:
Every `$PATH` scanner in the CLI also drops non-absolute entries. A relative
entry resolves against the process's working directory, which for a git hook is
whatever repository the caller was standing in, so a file committed to that
repository would otherwise be a binary Entire executes.

## Why agent instruction fields are local-only

`investigate.always_prompt` and every review `prompt` (per-agent and judge, in
`review_profiles` and the legacy `review` map) are appended verbatim to the
prompts of agents that `entire investigate` and `entire review` spawn with
approval checks disabled (claude-code's `bypassPermissions`, codex's
`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`). The prompt is the stated control
for those spawns, so whoever writes these strings gets the last word in it.
Honoring them from the committed `.entire/settings.json` would let an ordinary
pull request steer an approvals-disabled agent on every developer who pulls —
the same delivery route as the OPF [`command`](#why-command-is-local-only),
carrying instructions instead of argv.

They are therefore honored only from layers that are this developer's own:
clone-local review preferences (stored inside `.git/`, which a clone never
populates) or `.entire/settings.local.json` verified untracked in both the
index and `HEAD`. Rejection is a downgrade, never an error — agents still
receive the profile task and built-in defaults, and `entire review` /
`entire investigate` print a one-line notice naming the dropped field and where

content.text:
All five hardening items are implemented, tested, and verified. Everything is staged for your review — per your git workflow I'm waiting for your go-ahead before committing (and note: `commit.gpgsign=true` with your SSH security key means each commit will need a key touch — 5 commits planned).

## What was done

**1. redact — verify JSONL splices land.** One shared walk (`walkRedactableStrings`, copy-on-write) now feeds the splice collection, a post-splice verification, and a structural re-encode fallback, so the skip rules can't drift. Lines with replacements are decoded and checked against the recorded originals (honoring key scoping); a miss re-parses with `UseNumber` (large ints survive), redacts structurally, and re-encodes with `SetEscapeHTML(false)`, reattaching surrounding whitespace. A marshal failure fails the redaction, so `JSONLBytes` refuses to certify. I empirically confirmed the plan's premise (Go escapes U+2028 even with HTML escaping off). 10 regression tests, including a byte-identical fast-path pin.

**2. settings — provenance gate for agent instruction fields.** `enforceAgentPromptTrust` drops `investigate.always_prompt` and every `ReviewConfig.Prompt` (workers + judge, profiles + legacy map) unless developer-owned. Rejections are recorded on `AgentPromptRejections()` and `entire review`/`entire investigate` print a one-line stderr notice. A reflection test pins that any future `ReviewConfig` placement in the schema must be gated. Documented in `docs/security-and-privacy.md` and CLAUDE.md.

**3. checkpoint/remote — fetch-side ownership.** `FetchURL` now runs `checkpointRemoteIsInherited` (origin + the caller's read candidate as the identity set, reusing the push predicate verbatim) before deriving the checkpoint URL; on inherited it falls back to the read-candidate chain with `authoritative=false`, so ref-absence classification is unaffected.

**4. copilotcli — minimal tool surface.** `--allow-all-tools` replaced with `--deny-tool shell/write/url` (documented as automatic, prompt-free denials that outrank every allow), plus `--no-ask-user` and `--no-custom-instructions`. Verified against the installed Copilot CLI 1.0.81 (`copilot help permissions`, argv-acceptance probes — no auth exists here for a live call). Argv pinned by test; opt-in smoke test via `ENTIRE_COPILOT_SMOKE=1`.

**5. explain — shared terminal sanitizer.** `tuiutil.SanitizeTerminalText` (now strips whole ANSI/OSC sequences, keeps tabs/newlines); `checkpoint list` points at it and explain's verbose/full transcript rendering (content, tool name/detail, fallback text) passes through it at the display boundary — deliberately not inside `FormatCondensedTranscript`, which also builds LLM input.

## Judgment calls to review (per the "flag it, don't decide it" rule)

- **Clone-local preferences are a trusted layer for item 2** (deviation from the plan, which only named `settings.local.json`). They live in `.git/`, unreachable by clone, and are the review picker's migration target — gating them would break migrated users' prompts for zero security gain.
- **Review's own default-profile writer conflicts with the gate**: non-interactive first-run `entire review` saves default profiles *with prompts* into the committed project file (`setup` at `review/cmd.go:851`), which the gate then drops on the next load, with a recurring notice. Impact is soft (the profile Task carries the substance; the dropped prompt is boilerplate), but you may want that writer to stop persisting prompts to project scope, or move the default save to local scope. ## 1. The settings gate leaves `Task` open, which is most of the review threat
​
`ReviewConfig.Prompt` is gated; `ReviewProfileConfig.Task` is not. Both come from the same committed `.entire/settings.json`, and both land verbatim in the same prompt, adjacent — `review/prompt.go:42-52`:
​
```go
if trimmed := ...cfg.Task...; trimmed != "" {
    sections = append(sections, "Task: "+trimmed)      // ungated
    ...
}
if trimmed := ...cfg.AlwaysPrompt...; trimmed != "" {
    sections = append(sections, trimmed)               // gated by this PR
}
```
​
`profileTask` (`review/profile.go:59-62`) returns `cfg.Task` verbatim when set. So for `entire review`, a PR that writes its instructions into `task` instead of `prompt` gets the identical result — plus no rejection notice, because nothing was rejected. `review_default_profile` is ungated too, so a PR can also choose *which* profile runs. The commit message flags Task as "flagged rather than decided", but `docs/security-and-privacy.md` gives reasons for skills and model and none for task, which reads as an oversight rather than a decision.
​
Either gate `Task` (provenance is already computed per profile — it's one more `decide()` call) or say in the doc why the primary instruction channel is exempt when the field appended after it isn't.
​
Two things I checked that are *not* holes, worth recording so they don't get re-litigated:
- **`Skills` is genuinely safe**: `VerifyConfiguredSkillsInstalled` (`review/picker.go:1140-1174`) rejects any string that isn't a curated builtin or a discovered skill name, so free text there fails the run before the agent starts. The doc's "skills resolve to locally installed content" is backed by a real mechanism.
- **`investigate` has no equivalent gap**: `AlwaysPrompt` is `InvestigateConfig`'s only free-text field, so that half of the gate is complete.
​
## 2. `explain`'s "one sanitization point" doesn't cover the default output path
​
`formatTranscriptBytes` is the `--verbose`/`--full` path only. The default body isn't sanitized: `renderExplainBody` (`explain.go:2046-2049`) returns `md` **unmodified** when `shouldUseColor(w)` is false — piped output, `NO_COLOR`, any non-TTY — and the same raw-`md` fallback exists inline at `explain.go:2098-2099`. That `md` is built from the stored AI summary, or from `buildNoSummaryMarkdown(extractIntent(...), meta.FilesTouched, hint)`: agent-authored free text out of checkpoint metadata, which is the same trust class as the transcript content the commit does sanitize, and it's what most `explain` invocations print.
​
Worth also confirming glamour drops raw ESC from text nodes on the colored path rather than passing it into its own output.
​
## 3. The fetch-ownership blast radius is wider than "fork clone", and one doc line now says the opposite
​
`checkpointRemoteIsInherited` treats an undeterminable owner as inherited (`util.go:484-491`), so this isn't only forks: **any repo whose origin is a non-forge URL** — `file://`, a bare path, a host `gitremote.ParseURL` can't extract an owner from — now loses checkpoint reads with a committed `checkpoint_remote`. The PR's own integration test is the proof: `setupGitRefsCheckpointRemoteRepo` had to start writing a `settings.local.json`. Self-hosted/on-prem users hit this, and the PR body only names the fork case.
​
Relatedly, `util.go:456-458` still reads:
​
> An identity whose owner cannot be determined … counts as inherited: … and falling back **preserves the previous behavior for those repos**.
​
That was true while only `PushURL` used the predicate. For fetches it's now the reverse.
​
Also: the rejection is `logging.Warn` only, so reads silently return nothing and neither `status` nor `doctor` says why. Of the three rejection paths in this PR this is the one users will experience as "my checkpoints vanished", and it's the only one that didn't get a stderr notice. `entire status` already prints the checkpoint sync destination and its source — that's the natural place.
​
## 4. `copilotcli`: the "narrowest policy the CLI supports" claim is off
​
Verified on 1.0.83: all four flags exist, and `copilot help permissions` confirms *"Denial rules always take precedence over allow rules, even --allow-all-tools"* — so the deny approach is sound and a clear improvement on `--allow-all-tools`. But the same help text says the deny/allow flags *"control approval prompts and do not expose tools that were filtered out by `--available-tools`/`--excluded-tools`"*. Availability is a separate, stricter layer this PR doesn't touch, so read tools stay available and unprompted and untrusted transcript content can still steer file reads whose contents land in the generated summary. If the goal is really "nothing in the input may be able to drive tool execution", `--available-tools` is the control that does it. The claudecode path carries the same read residual, so this is a comment-accuracy fix plus an optional tightening, not a Copilot-specific regression.
​
Separate risk: "a text-only prompt completes without any approval flag" is validated only by the opt-in `ENTIRE_COPILOT_SMOKE=1` test that CI never runs. If that's wrong on some version or auth config, Copilot summaries degrade silently.
​
## 5. `redact`: solid — and measurably free
​
I benchmarked both commits on a 2000-line transcript with 3 secrets per line (M4 Max, `-count=3`):
​
|              | base `7e2f57fc6` | PR      |
| ------------ | ---------------- | ------- |
| secret-heavy | ~136 ms          | ~131 ms |
| no secrets   | ~89 ms           | ~86 ms  |
​
The verification re-parse is noise next to the regex layers, and the copy-on-write walk appears to pay for itself. Given redaction is a documented hot spot, that's worth stating in the PR body — otherwise a reader assumes a per-line re-parse costs something.
​
Two small things:
​
- **The "fails the redaction rather than certifying" contract has one call site where it doesn't.** `checkpoint/ephemeral.go:449-464` (subagent transcript) hard-fails only on `redact.ErrScannerDegraded`; any other `JSONLBytes` error is treated as "not valid JSONL" and downgraded to `redact.Bytes`. `reencodeRedacted` returns plain `fmt.Errorf`, so it takes the downgrade branch. This looks dormant in practice — the content already parsed once, and `Encode` over a map/`[]any`/string/`json.Number` tree can't realistically fail — but if the contract is meant to hold, that branch should key on a sentinel rather than on "any error means malformed JSONL".
- `redactJSONLLines`'s capacity comment ("Redaction only ever shrinks or preserves length") is now stale: `reencodeRedacted` can grow a line, since Go escapes U+2028/U+2029 unconditionally. It's only a `Grow` hint, so nothing breaks.

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit CLAUDE.md violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**Signal if uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** "Strange things are afoot at the Circle K"

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

## The Bottom Line

**External feedback = suggestions to evaluate, not orders to follow.**

Verify. Question. Then implement.

No performative agreement. Technical rigor always.

`investigate.always_prompt` and every review `prompt` (per-agent and judge, in

## Why agent instruction fields are local-only

`investigate.always_prompt`, every review `prompt` (per-agent and judge, in
`review_profiles` and the legacy `review` map), and every review profile's
`task` are placed verbatim in the prompts of agents that `entire investigate`
and `entire review` spawn with approval checks disabled (claude-code's
`bypassPermissions`, codex's `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`). The
prompt is the stated control for those spawns, so whoever writes these strings
gets the last word in it. `task` and `prompt` are adjacent sections of the same
composed prompt, so they are gated together — a gate on one alone would just
move the attacker's text to the other field. Honoring any of them from the
committed `.entire/settings.json` would let an ordinary pull request steer an
approvals-disabled agent on every developer who pulls — the same delivery route
as the OPF [`command`](#why-command-is-local-only), carrying instructions
instead of argv.

They are therefore honored only from layers that are this developer's own:
clone-local review preferences (stored inside `.git/`, which a clone never
populates) or `.entire/settings.local.json` verified untracked in both the
index and `HEAD`. Rejection is a downgrade, never an error — a dropped task
falls back to the built-in text for conventional profile names, and
`entire review` / `entire investigate` print a one-line notice naming the
dropped field and where it has to move (suppressed when the dropped task equals
the built-in default, since that drop changes nothing).

Deliberately not gated: `skills` (review validates every configured skill
against the locally installed set before spawning, so free text there fails the
run rather than reaching an agent), `agent` and `model` (registry keys and
routing hints, not instruction text), and `review_default_profile` (it only
selects among profiles whose instruction content is itself gated).

308	
309	// checkpointSyncInfo is the single shared computation behind both the text and
310	// JSON checkpoint-sync sections of `entire status`, so the two outputs cannot
311	// drift. Everything here reads local state only (settings, .git/config, local
312	// refs, the push queue) — status must stay network-free.
313	type checkpointSyncInfo struct {
314		// Remote is the elected git remote name, or the org/repo slug in
315		// dedicated checkpoint_remote mode. Empty when nothing resolved (no
316		// remotes configured, or the fail-closed case).
317		Remote string
318		// Source is config|observed|default|sole|first (resolver values) or
319		// "dedicated".
320		Source string
321		// Err is the fail-closed misconfiguration message from the resolver.
322		Err string
323		// Unpushed approximates checkpoints not yet on the sync destination; 0
324		// when none, when counting failed, or when the count would be a lie
325		// (dedicated URL mode on the git-branch backend).
326		Unpushed int
327	}

329	func computeCheckpointSyncInfo(ctx context.Context, s *EntireSettings) checkpointSyncInfo {
330		elected, err := strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)
331		if err != nil {
332			// Fail-closed: checkpoint_push_remote names a remote that does not
333			// exist. The pre-push gate is silently skipping checkpoint sync, so
334			// status is the user's signal.
335			// Accepted divergence: if a structured checkpoint_remote is also
336			// configured, the gate's dedicated exemption may still sync checkpoint
337			// data even while this fail-closed warning is shown, since there is no
338			// elected remote left to probe PushURL against here.
339			return checkpointSyncInfo{Err: err.Error()}
340		}
341		if elected.Name == "" {
342			return checkpointSyncInfo{} // no remotes configured: show nothing
343		}
344	
345		// Dedicated checkpoint_remote mode is reported only when PushURL derives
346		// an eligible URL for the elected remote, mirroring the pre-push
347		// exemption (ps.hasCheckpointURL); otherwise the gate applies normal
348		// single-remote sync, so status reports that instead. PushURL is
349		// local-only; never call resolvePushSettings here — its follow-up
350		// metadata fetch dials, and status must stay network-free.
351		// Accepted divergence: a real push to a different named remote may derive
352		// PushURL differently than this elected-remote probe does.
353		if cr := s.GetCheckpointRemote(); cr != nil {
354			if _, enabled, purlErr := checkpointremote.PushURL(ctx, elected.Name); purlErr == nil && enabled {
355				info := checkpointSyncInfo{Remote: cr.Repo, Source: checkpointSyncSourceDedicated}
356				// The unpushed counter is meaningful here only on the git-refs
357				// backend (push-queue length is local and accurate). The
358				// git-branch comparison is omitted: pushes to a raw URL update
359				// no remote-tracking ref, so it would permanently read "all
360				// unpushed".
361				if cpCfg, cfgErr := settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig(ctx); cfgErr == nil && checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs(cpCfg) {
362					info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, "")
363				}
364				return info
365			}
366		}
367	
368		return checkpointSyncInfo{
369			Remote:   elected.Name,
370			Source:   string(elected.Source),
371			Unpushed: countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, elected.Name),
372		}
373	}
374	
375	// countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus counts best-effort: status must never fail
376	// because counting failed, so errors log at debug and read as "no counter".
377	func countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx context.Context, remoteName string) int {
378		n, err := strategy.CountUnpushedCheckpoints(ctx, remoteName)
379		if err != nil {
380			logging.Debug(ctx, "unpushed checkpoint count failed; omitting from status",
381				slog.String("error", err.Error()))
382			return 0
383		}
384		return n
385	}
386	
387	// writeCheckpointSyncLines appends the checkpoint sync destination line (and
388	// the unpushed counter, when non-zero) to the enabled status block. Rendered
389	// whenever something resolved: an elected remote, a dedicated store, or the
390	// fail-closed misconfiguration. No remotes configured -> no lines.
391	func writeCheckpointSyncLines(ctx context.Context, b *strings.Builder, s *EntireSettings, sty statusStyles) {
392		info := computeCheckpointSyncInfo(ctx, s)
393		switch {
394		case info.Err != "":
395			b.WriteString("\n")
396			b.WriteString(sty.render(sty.yellow, "  ! Checkpoints NOT syncing: "+info.Err))
397		case info.Remote == "":
398			return
399		case info.Source == checkpointSyncSourceDedicated:
400			b.WriteString("\n  Checkpoints sync to: ")
401			b.WriteString(sty.render(sty.cyan, "dedicated checkpoint remote ("+info.Remote+")"))
402		default:
403			b.WriteString("\n  Checkpoints sync to: ")
404			b.WriteString(sty.render(sty.cyan, info.Remote))
405			switch info.Source {
406			case string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceConfig):
407				b.WriteString(sty.render(sty.dim, " (set by checkpoint_push_remote)"))
408			case string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceObserved):
409				b.WriteString(sty.render(sty.dim, " (follows your branch's push destination)"))
410			}
411		}
412		if info.Unpushed > 0 {
413			b.WriteString("\n  ")
414			b.WriteString(sty.render(sty.dim, formatUnpushedCheckpointsLine(info)))
415		}
416	}
417	
418	// formatUnpushedCheckpointsLine phrases the unpushed counter. Dedicated URL
419	// mode has no git remote to name (and only reaches here on the git-refs
420	// backend), so it drops the remote-name phrasing.
421	func formatUnpushedCheckpointsLine(info checkpointSyncInfo) string {
422		noun := "checkpoints"
423		pronoun := "they sync"
424		if info.Unpushed == 1 {
425			noun = "checkpoint"
426			pronoun = "it syncs"
427		}
428		if info.Source == checkpointSyncSourceDedicated {
429			return fmt.Sprintf("%d %s not yet pushed", info.Unpushed, noun)
430		}
431		return fmt.Sprintf("%d %s not yet on %s — %s with your next 'git push %s'",
432			info.Unpushed, noun, info.Remote, pronoun, info.Remote)
433	}

436	func timeAgo(t time.Time) string {
437		return formatRelativeDuration(time.Since(t))
438	}

- `a1fd6a56a` settings — body still says the profile **Task stays ungated**, which the fixup reversed (this is the one that genuinely misleads)

Clearing an untrusted ReviewConfig.Prompt makes prompt-only workers look unset. IsZero treats a config with only a now-empty prompt as empty, and nonZeroAgentConfigs then drops those workers. A committed Pi-style {"pi":{"prompt":"..."}} reviewer disappears after load, and a profile that only had such workers fails in selectReviewProfile before the new drop notice can print.

The fetchOwnershipURLs helper passes the wrong error to checkpointRemoteIsInherited. When getRemoteURL(ctx, lead) fails, the error is silently discarded and fetchOwnershipURLs returns nil. This means a transient error (network timeout, invalid git state) can make the ownership check incorrectly classify a legitimate checkpoint_remote as inherited, causing the fetch to silently fall back to origin and potentially read stale checkpoints. The function should either propagate the error up through fetchURLAuthoritative or at minimum log it, matching the push side's error handling for remote URL resolution.

Both findings verified with one nuance each:

- **Prompt-only workers**: confirmed — `IsZero` makes a gated-empty `{"pi":{"prompt":"..."}}` worker vanish in `nonZeroAgentConfigs`, and `selectReviewProfile` fails before the notice prints. Fix inside the gate itself: when clearing the prompt would zero the config, set `Agent` to the map key — semantically a no-op (empty `Agent` already means "the key is the agent name"), so the worker stays present and runs on the profile task.
- **`fetchOwnershipURLs`**: the exact "silently read stale from origin" scenario is narrower than stated (a missing lead can only *weaken* the check), but the real defect stands and is worse in the other direction: swallowing the error fails **open** — a differently-owned lead that transiently fails to resolve stops vetoing. The predicate's documented rule is "an identity whose owner cannot be determined counts as inherited", so a resolution failure should count as inherited (fail closed, logged), matching how the push side never routes to the checkpoint remote when its URL set can't be read.

Implementing both.
